chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Said from Safwan and Fadala from al-Ala' ibn Razin from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) and Safwan from Mansur ibn Hazim from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) that the two said: Regarding

two men, each of whom had food with the other, and each did not know how much he had with the other. So each said to his companion: 'What is with you is yours, and what is with me is mine.' He said: 'There is no harm in that if they mutually agreed.' And Mansur said in his narration: 'And their souls were pleased with it.'

key_terms.تَرَاضَيَا: they mutually agreed (from radhiya, implying consent and satisfaction)
key_terms.صَاحِبٌ: companion/owner (referring to the other party in the transaction)
key_terms.طَابَتْ بِهِ أَنْفُسُهُمَا: their souls were pleased with it (indicating genuine contentment and lack of grievance)
key_terms.طَعَامٌ: food (used here as a general term for sustenance or property held)
key_terms.لاَ بَأْسَ: there is no harm (a legal term indicating permissibility without strict obligation)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling for settling mutual debts when the exact quantities are unknown?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* highlights the flexibility of Islamic commercial law in resolving ambiguous debts through mutual consent (*taradun*), a principle deeply valued in Shia jurisprudence for preventing disputes. The inclusion of 'contentment of souls' (*tabat bihi anfusuhuma*) underscores that the validity of such settlements relies not just on legal technicalities but on the genuine satisfaction of both parties, reflecting the ethical spirit of the Sunnah.
